guideTitle: 5 Best Fruit Pickers with Baskets in 2026
metaTitle: Best Fruit Pickers with Baskets in 2026
metaDescription: Five fruit pickers with catch baskets compared, covering basket size, padding and pole length so soft fruit lands unbruised and your arms stay comfortable.
introParagraphs: When you shop for a fruit picker, the pole gets all the attention, but the basket is the part that actually touches your harvest. A good basket catches the fruit as it lets go of the stem, cushions the landing and holds enough to make a few trips unnecessary. A poor one lets oranges roll out the side, bruises peaches against bare wire or tips over under a heavy mango. This guide ranks five fruit pickers that come with their basket already attached, and judges each one by what the basket does.

The five picks cover different pole lengths but share the same basic idea of a metal head that twists onto the shaft. The two DonSail poles carry a roomy basket with a short claw. The BlumeTrec 6.5FT is a compact pole with a foam-lined cup. The Walensee 13FT adds a cushioned pad at extra reach, and the SKGPOLE 26FT pairs a 5.5 inch diameter basket with a very tall aluminum pole.

We evaluated every pick from its listing specs and the way buyers describe daily use, so sizes and materials are as the makers state them. We left out basket-only heads and accessories, since they need a pole you may not own. If you already have a threaded pole, the notes on thread size in this guide will help you match a replacement head. Whatever you choose, remember that the best basket is the one you can aim comfortably, because a perfectly designed cup is no use if the pole is too awkward to place under the fruit.

products.name: DonSail Fruit Picker Pole with Basket, 35 to 150 Inch
specs: Metal twist-on basket about 9 by 5.5 by 5.5 inches
products.description:
The DonSail 35 to 150 inch model wins this guide because its basket is the deepest of the group. The metal twist-on head measures about 9 by 5.5 by 5.5 inches, which is large enough for an orange, a pear or an avocado, and the maker lists apples, peaches and pecans too. The pole adjusts by sections from 35 up to 150 inches, so you pick how much reach you build.

A deep basket matters because it keeps fruit from rolling out when you tilt the pole. With a shallow cup, a second orange can knock the first one loose. Here the sides hold the fruit while you lower the pole, and a full basket still fits through branches without snagging. The thick 1 inch stainless steel shaft is stiff enough that the head does not whip around.

The tradeoff is heft at the top. A big basket plus a long steel shaft can feel tip-heavy once it is loaded with a few pomelos, so shorten the pole when you can. Compared with the SKGPOLE, the DonSail has a roomier basket but a much shorter maximum reach. It is the pick for people who mostly want to harvest citrus and pears from medium trees. In use, tip the pole slightly toward you as you lower it so gravity keeps the fruit against the back of the cup. At 150 inches it reaches almost twice as far as the 77 inch BlumeTrec 6.5FT, which is why it suits taller citrus. Rinse the head after a sticky citrus session so juice does not dry on the wire.
products.bestFor: Citrus and pears from medium trees where a deep basket keeps fruit from rolling out.
cons: Tip-heavy when full at long length

products.name: DonSail Fruit Picker Pole with Basket and Claw, 35 to 65 Inch
products.description:
The short DonSail takes the same basket idea and puts it on a pole of 35 to 65 inches. The listing calls it a fruit picker rake with a metal basket head and claw, suitable for avocados, tangerines and other small to medium fruit. The pole sections can be set at lengths of about 3 to 5 feet.

What the claw adds is a way to hook a stem. Instead of lifting the basket under a fruit, you can catch the stem with the claw and twist it free. That is useful for tangerines and small avocados that hang in clusters. The shorter pole means the basket is easy to aim, which is a real advantage when the fruit sits among thick leaves.

It is the least tiring pole to use because at 65 inches the weight is held close to your body. The price of that comfort is reach: you will be standing near the tree, not reaching into its crown. Compared with the 35 to 150 inch DonSail, it is for low fruit only. A practical trick is to work from the outside of the tree inward, hooking the claw behind the stem and giving a quarter twist. Keep a small bucket at your feet so you can drop fruit in without bending. At 65 inches maximum it is 85 inches shorter than the long DonSail, so treat it as a companion pole and not a replacement.
products.bestFor: Low-hanging tangerines, avocados and small fruit among dense leaves.
pros: Short pole is easy to aim
Light enough to hold for a long time
Same sturdy shaft as the larger model

products.name: BlumeTrec 6.5FT Fruit Picker with Basket
specs: Thick foam pad at basket bottom
products.description:
The BlumeTrec 6.5FT pairs a compact pole with a foam-lined basket. The pole runs from 35 to 77 inches in 16 inch sections, and a thick foam pad at the bottom of the basket gives picked fruit a soft landing, which the listing says helps reduce impact and damage.

The foam is the feature that matters for apples and peaches. A bare wire floor bruises thin skin in a single drop, while foam spreads the shock. With this pole you get that protection in a short, controllable size that suits dwarf trees and trained fruit.

Compared with the DonSail 35 to 150 inch model, the BlumeTrec holds less and reaches less. It is a better match for gentle handling than for volume. It is also a good complement: the same maker sells a 13.5 foot version for taller trees. Choose this one if you prioritize the condition of each piece of fruit. Set the pole at a length where your arms stay below shoulder height, since overhead work tires you fast. Its 77 inch top end is only 12 inches longer than the short DonSail's 65, so the real difference between those two is a foam pad versus a claw. Replace the foam pad if it flattens or tears, because a worn pad loses its cushioning.
products.bestFor: Dwarf apples and peaches where bruising is the main worry.
pros: Thick foam pad cushions each drop
Easy to store in 16 inch pieces

products.name: Walensee 13FT Fruit Picker Pole with Basket
products.description:
The Walensee 13FT places a cushioned basket at the end of a telescoping pole that extends from 35 to 158 inches. The listing says the foam pad absorbs impact when fruit drops, helping reduce bruising, and the pole is built from reinforced stainless steel. It is marketed as a mango picker, which hints at its capacity for heavier fruit.

Combining a soft basket with extra reach is the main appeal. You can pick from a tall tree and still protect the fruit. The shorter 5.5 foot Walensee model is also sold, so you can match the pole to your tree.

The cost is the same one every long steel pole carries: weight at the tip and conductivity near wires. Compared with the SKGPOLE, the Walensee is heavier but has the foam pad and stainless build. Choose it when you want protection for your fruit at height. A cushioned head is especially welcome on a tall pole, because a longer drop means a harder landing. Let the telescoping sections click fully into place before you lift, and wipe them dry before storage. Its 158 inches is only 8 inches more than the long DonSail's 150, so the foam pad is the real reason to choose it over that model.
products.bestFor: Tall mango and apple trees where fruit condition still matters.
cons: Metal pole is risky near lines

products.name: SKGPOLE 26FT Reach Fruit Picker
products.description:
The SKGPOLE is the reach champion in the lineup. Its aluminum telescoping pole runs from 5 to 20 feet and the maker states a reach of up to 26 feet, while the large metal basket has a 5.5 inch diameter and an ultra thick foam pad. The thread is 3/4 inch American standard, so the head screws on the way most extension poles do.

The 5.5 inch basket is smaller than the DonSail's deep cup, so it suits apples, pears and smaller citrus better than grapefruit. The foam pad is thick, and the aluminum shaft keeps the tip lighter than a steel pole of the same length.

Reach is the reason to buy it, but reach brings risk. Aluminum conducts electricity extremely well, and a pole this tall can touch a wire before you notice. Compared with the Walensee, the SKGPOLE lifts the basket several feet higher and weighs less. Use it only when the tree demands it. Plan where your feet will be before you extend it fully, because it is awkward to reposition a 20 foot pole with fruit on the end. Lower it, empty the basket, and then move. Because the thread is the common 3/4 inch American standard, the head screws on the way most extension poles do, so replacing a cracked basket is simple.
products.bestFor: Tall fruit trees where light weight and height outweigh basket size.
pros: Reach up to 26 feet by the maker's claim

buyingCriteria.explanation: A deeper basket holds fruit while you lower the pole. The DonSail basket measures about 9 by 5.5 by 5.5 inches, while the SKGPOLE basket is 5.5 inches across. Large citrus needs a roomy cup. If you pick small fruit like tangerines, a smaller basket is fine. As a rule of thumb, a basket should be wide enough to slide under the fruit with a little space to spare. If it is too tight, you will knock neighboring fruit loose as you work.

Foam or sponge protects fruit from the wire floor. The BlumeTrec, Walensee and SKGPOLE all list a foam pad. Without padding, thin-skinned fruit bruises on landing. Look for a pad that is thick and glued, not loose. Foam pads are glued in, so check whether the pad is easy to replace. A flattened pad should be swapped before the next season.

Some heads have claws or prongs to hook stems, like the short DonSail. Others have an open mouth you push upward. Claws help with clusters and small fruit. Open baskets are quicker for large single pieces. For gardeners with a weak grip, an open basket requires less twisting than a claw. A claw, on the other hand, helps when the fruit is hidden behind leaves.

The DonSail short pole spans 35 to 65 inches, the BlumeTrec 6.5FT reaches 77 inches, the DonSail long reaches 150 inches, the Walensee 158 inches, and the SKGPOLE up to 20 feet. A heavy basket at the end of a long lever tires the arms. Match the pole to the tree and avoid extra length. If you are choosing between two lengths, go with the shorter one and add a second pole later. The short DonSail at 65 inches suits that approach, because it handles low branches and can sit beside the 150 inch model for the rest.

The SKGPOLE uses a 3/4 inch American standard thread, and other heads in this class often fit the same size. Knowing your thread lets you replace a damaged head without replacing the pole. Check that the basket twists on firmly and does not wobble. Match the thread size and tighten the head by hand before every session. A loose head can come off at the worst moment and drop onto the ground or onto you.

Every pole here is metal, and all conduct electricity. Never raise one near an overhead line, and keep well clear in wet weather. If a tree is tangled in wires, leave it to a professional. Safety outranks every other criterion. Check the area above you for wires, branches, and low roofs, and plan your path so that you never swing the pole sideways. If you cannot see all the way up, do not extend the pole.

howWeEvaluated.title: Basket capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stated basket sizes. The DonSail head measures about 9 by 5.5 by 5.5 inches, while the SKGPOLE basket is 5.5 inches across. Deeper baskets scored higher for citrus. The long DonSail led here for roomy citrus capacity, while the 5.5 inch SKGPOLE head was marked down for large fruit like grapefruit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fruit protection
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked padding. The BlumeTrec, Walensee and SKGPOLE list foam pads, and the DonSail uses a metal basket with a claw option. Cushioning mattered most for soft fruit. Foam was the clear differentiator for soft fruit, so the BlumeTrec 6.5FT, with its short, controllable pole and foam pad, ranked well for peaches.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared maximum reach, from 65 inches on the short DonSail to up to 26 feet on the SKGPOLE. Each pick was matched to a typical tree height. The SKGPOLE and Walensee lead on height, and the short DonSail is the easiest to hold. Reach alone did not decide rank, since a pole that outruns your tree only adds weight.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored lighter poles for long reach and sturdy shafts for short ones. Aluminum and steel were weighed against each other. Steel feels stiffer, which suits the DonSail and Walensee, and aluminum feels lighter, which is what lets the SKGPOLE reach 20 feet without becoming unmanageable.

howWeEvaluated.title: Compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We noted threads and attachment, including the 3/4 inch standard on the SKGPOLE, so a head can be replaced. Only the SKGPOLE states its thread, so it earned the compatibility point, and the other poles were scored on how easily their heads twist on.

faq.q: What size basket do I need?
faq.a: For oranges and grapefruit, choose a deep basket like the DonSail at about 9 by 5.5 by 5.5 inches. For apples and small fruit, a 5.5 inch basket such as the SKGPOLE is enough. Match the basket to the biggest fruit you pick. Test the fit with the biggest fruit you expect to pick. If you grow several kinds of fruit, consider two poles instead of one.

Yes, it cushions the landing and reduces bruising, especially for peaches and apples. The BlumeTrec, Walensee and SKGPOLE list foam. A bare wire floor can bruise thin skin. Foam wears down with use, so check it each season. Some gardeners add a layer of soft cloth, though a built-in pad is neater.

faq.q: Can I replace just the basket?
faq.a: Often yes, if the thread matches. The SKGPOLE uses a 3/4 inch American standard thread. Check the thread before buying a separate head. A mismatch is the most common reason a new head will not fit.

faq.q: How do I pick without damaging the tree?
faq.a: Lift the basket under the fruit and twist gently so the stem releases. Do not pull branches down. Leave unripe fruit on the tree. Take your time, because rushing leads to broken branches. A steady, slow lift always works better than a quick jerk.

faq.q: Are these safe near power lines?
faq.a: No. All of these poles are metal and conduct electricity. Look up before you extend any pole, and keep well away from lines. Call the utility if a tree touches a wire. The 20 foot SKGPOLE and 158 inch Walensee are the two where this check matters most.

faq.q: How do I clean the basket?
faq.a: Rinse off juice and sap with warm water and let it dry. Sugar attracts insects and can gum up threads. Store the pole dry. A soft brush helps with stubborn sap.
